summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework sets what a trans visitor faces at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry. Airport screening follows federal procedure: Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and trigger secondary screening and pat-downs, and travellers may request alternative screening or decline the scanner.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

The territorial layer runs the other way. The Virgin Islands human-rights law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the Attorney General ruled that the territory's anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, an official interpretation extending territorial protections. Same-sex marriage has been legal since a 2015 territorial Superior Court ruling struck down the denial of marriage licences to same-sex couples, later settled nationwide by federal recognition. The historic sodomy statute, applied from 1957, has been replaced. None of this alters federal document rules, federal screening, or federal funding decisions, and no territorial statute softens them.
tangentialFactors:
The territory is small and has no independent document or border regime, so the 2025 federal turn is felt through it directly: marker disputes and screening friction arise from national policy rather than from any local enactment. Local reporting in July 2017 described the LGBTQ community in the territory as seeing losses alongside reason for hope, which indicates a protection framework that has been contested rather than settled in practice.

The contrast between layers is the main turbulence a visitor should expect. Territorial protections on gender identity and the 2017 Attorney General interpretation sit beneath a national document regime, a national screening procedure and national funding and visa decisions that operate independently of them, so a visitor can be simultaneously protected against private discrimination and exposed at the federal touchpoints of entry, screening, care funding and, for athletes, visa issuance.
localsOnly:
Residents of the U.S. Virgin Islands are covered by the territory's human-rights law, which prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, and by the March 2017 Attorney General ruling that this anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students in territorial schools.

Same-sex marriage has been available in the territory since the 2015 territorial Superior Court ruling that found the denial of marriage licences unconstitutional, and the question was later settled nationwide by federal recognition. The sodomy statute applied from 1957 has been replaced.

Residents holding United States travel documents are subject to the same federal document rules as any other United States national, including the January 2025 elimination of the X marker, and to federal airport screening procedure when travelling.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how the January 2025 executive order eliminating the X marker has been applied in practice to documents issued to residents of the U.S. Virgin Islands, or whether any territorial court has considered it; that remains unresolved here.

The inventory does not establish whether the federal funding order on gender-affirming care has affected any specific territorial hospital or clinic, so the reach of that order within the territory is stated only at the level of federally funded institutions generally.

Enforcement of the territorial anti-discrimination law in relation to transgender adults, as distinct from the 2017 ruling on students, is not sourced, and no source in the inventory records trans-specific violence incidents, outcomes or police response in the territory.
